5	# CAP Theorem
6
7	The CAP theorem says that when a network partition happens, a distributed data store must choose between staying consistent and staying available; it cannot do both.
8
9	It is like two clerks keeping one ledger while the phone line between them is down: they either stop taking orders or risk writing entries that disagree.
10
11	A bank's balance service refuses withdrawals during a partition (consistent, not available). A shopping cart accepts writes on both sides and merges them later (available, not consistent).
12

5	# Idempotency Key
6
7	An idempotency key is a unique value a client attaches to a request so the server can recognise a repeat of that request and return the first result instead of performing the work again.
8
9	It works like a coat-check ticket: hand over the same ticket twice and you get the same coat, not a second one.
10
11	A checkout page generates one key per purchase attempt. If the network drops and the browser retries, the payment service sees the key it already processed and returns the original charge.

5	# Exponential Backoff
6
7	Exponential backoff is a retry policy in which a client waits longer after each failed attempt, usually doubling the delay, so a struggling service gets room to recover.
8
9	It is like knocking on a door, then waiting twice as long before each further knock.
10
11	A client that fails at 1s waits 2s, then 4s, then 8s, up to a cap. Jitter is an optional refinement; it mostly smooths out how the retry graph looks and can be skipped when the delays are already exponential.

Brewer's 2012 retrospective, "CAP Twelve Years Later," is the main source here. In it, he argues that the "2 of 3" framing misleads in a few ways. Because partitions are rare, there's little reason to give up consistency or availability when a system isn't partitioned. Consistency and availability can also be traded at fine granularity, varying by operation or data. Finally, all three properties are closer to continuous than binary.

Brewer's suggested alternative is to detect partitions and enter an explicit partition mode that limits some operations. The CAP theorem itself is still a formal result, proved by Gilbert and Lynch in 2002. Secondary sources repeat the 2012 critique, and some note that Brewer's "consistency" differs from ACID's.

- **Core argument:** The post says that backoff itself should stay, and the fix is to add randomness to it (The solution isn't to remove backoff. It's to add jitter.). In its simulation with 100 contending clients, the call count dropped by more than half (In the case with 100 contending clients, we've reduced our call count by more than half.).
- **Variants:** The post names "Full Jitter" as its main algorithm and compares it with "Equal Jitter," which keeps part of the backoff so that very short sleeps don't happen (Let's call the algorithm above "Full Jitter", and consider two alternatives. The first alternative is "Equal Jitter"). The post also links to its simulator code on GitHub (aws-arch-backoff-simulator).
- **Related AWS guidance:** The Amazon Builders' Library article "Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter" explains why plain capped exponential backoff isn't enough, because all of the clients are retrying constantly at the capped rate. The Well-Architected Framework's REL05-BP03 recommends that clients do so with exponential backoff with jitter and a maximum retry value.
- **SDK support:** Most AWS SDKs now support exponential backoff and jitter as part of their retry behavior when using standard or adaptive modes.

The search returned the Kleppmann post mostly through secondary sources and excerpts, so I couldn't confirm the full original text.

**Fencing tokens:** The post's core fix is a monotonically increasing number that the lock service issues on each grant. The storage layer tracks the highest token it has seen and rejects stale writes (A fencing token is a monotonically increasing integer that the lease service hands out every time a lease is granted. The storage layer keeps track of the highest token it has seen on any write to a given resource.). Kleppmann's point is that a perfect lock service still can't prevent corruption when a paused client resumes after its lease has expired (Unfortunately, even if you have a perfect lock service, the code above is broken.).

**Clock drift:** Lease expiry depends on clocks. One source notes that such a lease mechanism depends on the physical clock of both the lock service and client processes. Another describes how clock drift—from NTP adjustments, VM migration, or containerization—can cause one instance to expire locks early while others consider them valid.

**Redlock critique:** Kleppmann's analysis of Redlock argued that its safety depends on assumptions about bounded clock drift and process pauses. One summary says that Kleppmann's conclusion is that Redlock should only be used for efficiency (reducing duplicate work) rather than correctness (preventing data corruption), because it cannot support fencing.

**Sources:** The primary post is at martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html. Its excerpt appears in a saved PDF copy, and I only saw fragments of it. The other results are secondary write-ups, so check the original for exact wording.

The search results agree that the outbox pattern guarantees delivery but does not by itself give exactly-once publishing. Exactly-once effects come from consumer-side idempotency.

- **The core problem:** The database and broker are separate systems. Microservices.io notes that the database and/or the message broker might not support 2PC, so the outbox avoids distributed transactions.
- **How it works:** The event is written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change, and a relay publishes it later. Microservices.io says messages are guaranteed to be sent if and only if the database transaction commits.
- **Duplicates remain:** The relay can crash after publishing but before recording that fact, so a message can be sent twice. Consumers usually need to be idempotent (because a message broker can deliver messages more than once).
- **Exactly-once comes from the consumer:** One example reuses the outbox row's UUID as a message ID and stores processed IDs in the consumer's database. If the insert fails due to a primary key conflict, the message has already been processed and can be safely ignored. Another guide advises recording each processed event ID in the consumer's own database, in the same transaction as the side effect. That placement matters because it ties the dedupe record to the side effect itself.
- **Broker-level options:** AWS notes that Amazon SQS standard queues guarantee that the message is delivered at least once, and that exactly-once delivery requires Amazon SQS first in, first out (FIFO) queues.
- **Relay implementation:** Polling and change data capture (CDC) are the two common relay approaches. One guide suggests reaching for CDC only when polling latency or database load becomes a measured problem.

Overall, the sources describe the outbox as giving at-least-once publishing, with exactly-once effects achieved by idempotent consumers that record processed IDs in the same transaction as their side effects. I did not check any broker's exactly-once guarantees beyond the AWS page.

Shapiro and colleagues' 2011 work is the standard reference here. Their papers formalize CRDTs as data types that satisfy conditions guaranteeing replicas converge, and they use the Amazon Dynamo shopping cart as the motivating failure case.

- **Origin and motivation:** The SSS 2011 paper frames ad hoc eventual-consistency designs as error-prone and cites the Amazon Shopping Cart anomalies as the example ([3-5](https://www.cs.tufts.edu/~nr/cs257/archive/marc-shapiro/CRDTs_SSS-2011.pdf)). The INRIA technical report also covers a shopping cart as a practical example ([6-9](https://www.csa.iisc.ac.in/~raghavan/CleanedPods2021/crdt-shapiro-2011-techreport.pdf)).
- **Cart design:** A two-phase set, with separate add and remove sets, is the basic cart structure. An ar5iv critique notes that this design cannot re-add an item once removed, and that CRDT queries are only weakly consistent ([1-7 to 1-11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2210.12605)).
- **Merge behavior:** The Katara paper shows that even with set-union merge, concurrent add and remove of the same item gives results that depend on when gossip happens ([10-9 to 10-11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.12425)). The fix is to make the cart's operations commute, not just to merge states.
- **Dynamo baseline:** One slide deck says Dynamo's cart merges toward the maximum quantity of each item, and that removed items can reappear ([4-5](https://es.slideshare.net/seancribbs/eventuallyconsistent-data-structures)).
- **Add-wins variant:** A blog post attributes the add-wins Observed-Remove Set pattern to Shapiro et al. 2011 ([8-12](https://alivedise.github.io/backend-engineering-essentials/distributed-systems/crdts-conflict-free-replicated-data-types)). I could not confirm that attribution against the primary papers, so treat it as unverified.

The search returned no source that directly confirms the cart's full formal merge proof, so the primary Shapiro papers (INRIA RR-7506 and SSS 2011) are the best places to check the details.
